column1: # Starter knowledge for the WindowsFoldersDetector example (docs/ADDING_DETECTORS.md).
# Keyed on the lowercase leaf name, so "C:\Windows" and "Windows" both match.

column5: description
The OS itself: kernel, drivers, System32.
Default install location for 64-bit software.
Default install location for 32-bit software on a 64-bit OS.
Application data shared by all users. Hidden by default, and a common place for software to keep configuration - and for malware to keep itself.
Home directories. Replaced "Documents and Settings".
On Vista and later this is only a junction kept for compatibility. A real directory here means a very old system or something imitating one.
Performance Monitor output. Usually empty - which is exactly why it gets used as a staging directory.
Per-user deleted files.
The XP-era recycle bin. Should not exist on a modern install.
Volume Shadow Copy and indexing data. Not readable even by administrators without taking ownership.
WinRE boot image.
Boot manager resources.
UEFI boot loaders.
IIS is installed. On a workstation that is worth a question, and wwwroot is a favourite webshell location.
A writable scratch directory at the root of the drive. Legitimate installers use it; so does everything else.
Left behind by Intel driver installers.
Left behind by AMD driver installers.
Left behind by NVIDIA driver installers.
Not a stock folder at the drive root. Usually an OEM image; confirm it.
Local Office installation source.
Vendor preload leftovers.
The previous Windows install after an upgrade. Full of readable user data and old credential stores.
Roaming/Local/LocalLow application data inside a user profile.
Core OS binaries and drivers. On 64-bit Windows this holds the 64-bit files.
The 32-bit system directory, despite the name.
